title: The Seven Bowls of God's Wrath
summary: Seven angels pour out seven bowls of God's wrath: sores on the beast's worshipers, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat, darkness on the beast's throne, the Euphrates dried up for the kings of the east, and finally a great earthquake and giant hail as a voice from the throne declares “It is done.” Angels and the altar affirm that God's judgments are just. Demonic spirits like frogs gather the kings of the earth to a place called Armageddon, and though people suffer, they curse God and do not repent.
story: Chapter 15 introduced the seven angels with the last plagues and showed the redeemed singing beside the sea. Now the bowls are poured out in swift succession, without the long interludes between sixth and seventh that interrupted the seals and trumpets. The bowls repeat the pattern of the trumpets (land, sea, rivers, sun, darkness, the Euphrates, then the cosmic end), but in full rather than partial measure. The seventh bowl brings Revelation to the brink of the end again, with Babylon the great receiving the cup of God's wrath. Chapters 17 and 18 will then slow down to show that fall in detail.
historical:
The Euphrates, dried up for the kings from the east, again evokes Rome's eastern frontier and the Parthian empire beyond it (compare 9:14). Readers in Asia feared invasion from that direction, and some interpreters connect the scene with the rumor that Nero would return at the head of eastern armies. There is an older background too: the Greek historian Herodotus says that Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC by diverting the Euphrates and entering along the riverbed. The drying of waters also recalls the Red Sea and the Jordan, which God dried up for Israel.

Earthquakes were real terrors in the province of Asia. Tacitus records one in AD 17 that destroyed twelve cities in a night, and Laodicea was leveled around AD 60 and rebuilt at its own expense. Megiddo was a fortified city in northern Israel guarding the pass into the Jezreel Valley, the great plain where armies met. Deborah and Barak defeated the Canaanite kings by the waters of Megiddo (Judges 5:19), and King Josiah of Judah was killed there by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29), a defeat Israel long mourned (Zechariah 12:11).
cultural:
The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores (Exodus 9:10), water turned to blood (Exodus 7:20), darkness (Exodus 10:22), frogs (Exodus 8:6), and hail (Exodus 9:24). As with Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened, the plagues do not lead to repentance. Frogs were ritually unclean animals under the law (Leviticus 11:10-12), and the three spirits that look like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, the unholy trinity of chapters 12 and 13, spreading deceptive words. The altar that speaks in verse 7 is the altar under which the martyrs cried out (6:9-10): their prayer for justice is being answered.

The hailstones are literally talent-weight, a talent being a large unit of weight often estimated at about 75 to 100 pounds; the BSB gives the sense as almost a hundred pounds each. Hail was a weapon of God in Israel's story, at the Egyptian plague and in Joshua's battle at Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11). A thief's coming was a common early Christian image for the suddenness of Christ's return (Matthew 24:43; 1 Thessalonians 5:2), and the warning to stay clothed recalls the letter to Laodicea, told to buy white garments to cover the shame of its nakedness (3:18).
literary: The bowls are told rapidly, with a refrain of pouring. The first four strike the same regions as the first four trumpets (earth, sea, rivers, sun), and the last three move to the beast's throne, the Euphrates, and the air. Two interludes of praise interrupt the destruction (vv. 5-7), declaring God just, and one interruption comes in Christ's own voice (v. 15), a warning and a beatitude addressed directly to the hearers. Three times the chapter notes that people cursed God (vv. 9, 11, 21), and twice that they did not repent (vv. 9, 11), an ironic refrain. The seventh bowl's loud voice, “It is done!”, is a single Greek word meaning it has come to pass, and it echoes, though with a different verb, Jesus' cry from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30). The chapter ends with the same storm-and-earthquake signs that close each series, now at their greatest.

outline.t: The command, and the first bowl: sores
Second bowl: the sea turned to blood
Third bowl: rivers turned to blood; God declared just
Fifth bowl: darkness on the beast's throne
Sixth bowl: the Euphrates dried and the kings gathered at Armageddon
Seventh bowl: It is done; earthquake, hail, and Babylon's cup

doctrines.note: The angel of the waters and the altar declare God's judgments true and just, because those who shed the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink. Judgment fits the crime, and God's justice answers the cries of the oppressed.

Three times the sufferers curse God, and twice we are told they refuse to repent. The chapter shows how deeply a heart can harden: pain can confirm a person in rebellion rather than break it. Repentance is a gift and a turning, not an automatic result of hardship.
In the middle of the bowls, Christ speaks: “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” The warning is also a promise. His return is certain, and those who stay awake and clothed are called blessed.

words.note: Dikaios, just, righteous. The angel calls God righteous and the altar calls his judgments “true and just”. In Scripture God's righteousness includes his faithfulness to set things right, to vindicate the wronged and to hold wrongdoers to account.
Blasphēmeō, to slander, speak evil of, blaspheme. The beast blasphemed God in 13:6, and now its followers do the same under judgment. The worshipers become like the one they worship.

Kleptēs, thief. Jesus compared his coming to a thief's coming (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and Peter repeat the image (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point is not secrecy but suddenness: those who are not watching will be caught unprepared.

Armageddōn, Armageddon, the Greek form of a Hebrew name. Most take it as Har Megiddo, mountain of Megiddo, though Megiddo stood in a plain and has no mountain as such. Others suggest a link with the mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13) or read it as a symbolic name for the place where the world's powers gather against God.

christ: In the middle of the bowls Christ himself speaks: “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” The verse turns a vision of cosmic judgment into a personal address. Jesus used the same image in the Gospels (Matthew 24:42-44), and it tells the churches that their Lord's return is the center around which all these judgments turn. The cry from the throne, “It is done!”, recalls in spirit the cry of the cross, where Jesus' work of redemption was completed. What was accomplished at the cross, the defeat of sin and the powers, is here brought to its full outworking in the world. The bowls also answer the martyrs at the altar (6:9-10), whose cry was for the Lord, holy and true, to act; the one who shed his own blood for others is the one before whom the shedding of innocent blood is finally judged.

hard.q: Is Armageddon a literal battle at a real place?
hard.a:
Readers answer differently. Many futurists expect a literal final gathering of armies in the region of Megiddo in northern Israel before Christ returns. Preterists often connect the imagery with the wars of the first century and the judgment of Rome or Jerusalem. Historicists have matched it to various conflicts in church history. Idealists and many others read Armageddon as a symbolic name: Megiddo was the classic battlefield of Israel's history, the place of both victory and tragic defeat, so the name evokes the final confrontation between God and the powers of the world, wherever and however it comes. They also note that no battle is actually described here; the kings are only gathered, and when the confrontation comes in 19:19-21 and 20:8-9, it is decided by Christ's word, not by armies.

Revelation has often been used to map its imagery onto the headlines of the reader's own time, and those maps have repeatedly failed. The chapter itself turns attention away from speculation to readiness: in the middle of the gathering of kings, Christ says to stay awake.

questions: Three times the people curse God, and they do not repent. What keeps a person from turning to God even when life is breaking down?
The altar where the martyrs cried out now declares God's judgments just. How does this chapter speak to people who have suffered injustice?
In the middle of the bowls, Jesus says to stay awake and clothed. What does spiritual wakefulness look like in an ordinary week?
